GenLayer CEO Albert Castellana on why AI agent commerce needs neutral escrow instead of the legal system

"The way we look at this is that these agents will want to not lose the money."

"They cannot believe in the legal system, just because of the cost and the slowness of it."

"If I have some sort of smart contract that can be holding the money as an escrow, and also evaluating the evidence in a neutral way, then that would be the safest way for me to not lose the money and be able to actually do commerce."

"It's a court for the Internet."

"I deploy the contract, I have negotiated offchain something with another agent, the money is transacted, it's put into the escrow, then the other agent will do some piece of work, and then it will be a neutral party that will decide who's right."

"I really think it's gonna be a lot of the agents just deploying the contracts and trying to resolve between them, as we do with humans. Now the problem with humans is just that the legal system is very, very archaic."

Super fun onchain right now, but it’s clear how this game ends:

100s of millions in USD are sitting in unrealized PnL, with very limited onchain liquidity.

FOMO trop uPnL traders are locked in (3,3) unwilling to sell: both to avoid nuking the tokens and because of potential reputational damage.

We're like in the air of inflated valuations and the fun can continue as long as there are new buyers and biggest holders don't sell.

but this meta will end like others before:

Attention will expand to copy-paste the same playbook from RH to Solana (currently happening) then potentially to Arc and then other venues. Maybe Base gets their shit together.

More and more tokens are being printed and while degen limited attention gets diluted the LP pools get thinner and USD flows per token are diluted as well.

All we need is some panic in the market and FOMO top players nuke their charts one by one because, well, 'everyone was selling. How could I hold?'

Similarly LPs, who are degen farming (like me) will withdraw liquidity the moment its needed the most.

Pools will get thinner and volatility will get worse. When memecoins nuke they get less interesting to buy because PRICE is the product.

(unlike revenue tokens which get more attractive as token prices go down).

But I'm not a boomer!

The game is fun right now.

But if you are sitting on huge gains, take profits. The temptation to keep rotating them to other coins is strong.

And LPs, consider selling rewards to stablecoins instead of putting them back to the pools.

This is insane! People's imagination for using memeFi is hitting new levels

You'll all be familiar with memes pumping real Penny Stonks, but not manipulating in game economies...

$RSTR is attempting to build a MicroStrategy-style treasury, except the reserve asset is Robin Hood hats inside Old School RuneScape

Why now? Because it's on Robonhood chain...

How it works:

1) $RSTR launched on pons against ETH
2) Every trade pays a 1% fee; of which 70% accrue to the token creator + 30% to pons
3) The RSTR operator claims the creator fees, converts the ETH into OSRS gold (assuming through Bond purchases?) uses that gold to buy Robin Hood hats
4) The hats are spread across multiple RuneScape accounts + withheld from sale
5) Removing hats from circulation pushes up the in-game market price, generating screenshots, attention and theoretically more $RSTR trading
6) More $RSTR trading produces more creator fees, funding further hat purchases

I wanted to check this against a third party source to see if this was actually happening... it is!

i) The GE tracker most players use in RuneScape is showing a spike from 700k RSGP to 4.5m now each hat in just two days
ii) The current price you can buy the hats for is > $4.5m RSGP... i checked and max bid to buy more of the supply actually in game (screenshot)

The main challenges to the process is that there's an element that needs to be off-chain with a human intermediary in using the ETH fees to purchase bonds + then in game currency for the RH hats

I'm not a lawyer but as long as they're purchasing the bonds through Jagex then it should be in compliance? Although not sure about intentional manipulation of in game economics?

Even so... if the accounts are banned it permanently removes the hats from the game and hence achieves the same outcome

You can capitalize on this by buying in game before it goes insane or more speculative through their token

Jagex would receive the revenue from Bond sales, but it's not public so we are unable to benefit from that side of the trade

Once again onchain mechanisms being used with memes to draw in more retail attention... this time from millions of RuneScape players!

A meme paired with a 3x short on $PONS is called "TAMPONS"... 

The mechanics for TAMPONS are pretty interesting:

1) Every $TAMPONS trade pays a 1% fee; part of that revenue is continuously routed into collateral backing a 3× short position on $PONS 

2) If PONS falls, the short generates a profit. The system periodically realizes part of it, then uses 75% of the proceeds to market-buy and burn TAMPONS

3) Flywheel: 

TAMPONS volume → fees → larger PONS short → realized profits if PONS falls → TAMPONS buybacks + burns

It isn’t a direct or fully redeemable hedge; holders don’t own the short or have a claim on its collateral. But structurally, TAMPONS converts trading activity & PONS downside into recurring buy pressure for itself

Japan spent dollars to defend the yen. Its gold defended Japan.

• Dollars had to be spent.
• Foreign securities had to be sold.
• Gold simply sat there and became more valuable.

When monetary stress arrived, Japan’s interest-bearing paper assets were depleted while the supposedly “unproductive” asset strengthened the country’s balance sheet.

Gold is no one else’s liability. It cannot default, be sanctioned into worthlessness or be printed to defend a currency. Japan bought no additional gold in August, yet gold became dramatically more important to Japan.

Gold is nevertheless easing around $4,403 today after strong US employment data lifted the probability of a September Fed hike to roughly 58%. That is a short-term interest-rate headwind, with US PPI and CPI now this week’s major tests.

Silver does not enjoy gold’s central-bank reserve demand, but it offers greater leverage if concerns over currencies, sovereign debt and declining real purchasing power drive investors back into hard assets.

Gold remains the monetary leader. Silver remains the higher-beta follower with a structurally depleted physical market.

The larger copper story remains unchanged: constrained mine supply, inadequate project development and accelerating demand from grids, electrification, data centres and AI infrastructure.

Paper reserves are spent. Gold reserves reprice.

Bitcoin ETFs pulled in roughly $3.54B in August.
ETH ETFs attracted about $1.84B over the same month.

But what about all the other altcoin ETFs? Is there actually demand beyond the big 2?

Here’s what I found:

One interesting date is August 28th.

Bitcoin ETFs saw roughly $202M in net outflows, but several other crypto ETFs were still attracting money.

ETH took in about $102M, XRP $26M, SOL $17.3M, and HYPE $4.5M.
One day isn’t enough of a sample size, though. 

Here’s how those four non-BTC categories looked across the full trading week of August 24–28:

• $ETH: +$815.7M
• $SOL: +$142.7M
• ripple:native: +$110.5M
• $HYPE: +$56.8M

Nice, so there was demand beyond BTC and ETH.

SOL and XRP both attracted more than $100M that week, and HYPE brought in another $57M.

Those three combined took in roughly $310M, although ETH still attracted way more than all 3 put together. 

But the following week is where the picture gets more interesting.

From August 31 through September 4, net inflows into the SOL funds tracked by Farside slowed to just $4.9M. HYPE’s fell to $12.3M.

Both were still positive for the week, but the pace was very different from what we’d just seen.

And that happened while Bitcoin ETFs attracted another $987M.

So there’s clearly demand beyond BTC and ETH, but I wouldn’t call it a broader trend yet. SOL and HYPE’s inflows slowed sharply the following week, even while BTC kept attracting money.

SOL, XRP, and HYPE are the ones I’m watching. I’m more interested in whether they can keep attracting money over the next month than how much they brought in during one strong week.

2 quick thoughts

1. I'm surprised Solana hasn't been attracting more inflows from TradFi
 
2. Not too excited for any other future altcoin ETFs. I don't see how they can move the needle if these aren't.

A new article reports that they received another 30 days to improve the offer and address the Israeli government’s concerns. The revised structure would give Israel greater control over $ZIM Israel, direct access to 16 new ships, and stronger protection of strategic shipping routes.

https://t.co/cEdugahZY3

OUR TAKE:

The stated buyout price is $35 per share, valuing $ZIM at approximately $4.2 billion. However, once you include employee compensation, the assets and part of the business being transferred to FIMI, and other expenses, Hapag-Lloyd is effectively paying around $45 per share. This means its models likely valued $ZIM at at least $60 per share when they made the offer.

And that valuation was calculated before the “golden swan” event we are now witnessing in shipping rates, which is nothing short of historic and re rating the entire industry. 

Why would Hapag-Lloyd pay so much? Because it understands that $ZIM is worth much more.

Take a pen and paper and add up all of $ZIM’s assets, cash, vessels, and long-term charter contracts. You can easily reach a sum-of-the-parts valuation of more than $100 per share.

But even that calculation understates the real value because many of these assets cannot simply be bought today, regardless of how much money you have. The average delivery time for a new container ship is more than three years, while many large LNG dual-fuel ships ordered today will not be delivered until 2029 or 2030.

Recreating $ZIM’s fleet, contracts, routes, and operating network would take years. That scarcity makes the whole company worth considerably more than the simple sum of its parts.

The original $35 bid was made when shipping rates were far lower. It is like bidding for an oil company when oil is at $60, while oil is now trading at $90.

At current rates, $ZIM will have more than $30 per share in cash by year-end, more than its entire current public market value ($28.5).

With aggressive buybacks and dividends, it is easy to see $ZIM doubling from here within the next few years while continuing to offer one of the highest dividend yields in the market.

- Biz / monetization models - less important for memes, and less impt in certain market conditions. will be important eventually

So, how much does it cost? Assuming Jensen means 100k GPUs, I looked up public rental prices for GB300 NVL72 and Verda lists $8.62 per GPU per hour.

That’s $862,000 an hour. $20.7 million a day. $620.6 million a month. So suppose the pre-training run is 3 months, running 24/7: $1.86 BILLION!! 

And then, obviously, they still need to do a lot of post-training. Obviously, you cannot just add 100,000 GPUs to your cart and click checkout. And yes, you probably negotiate a much better price when buying in bulk so this is a public list price ballpark, not the actual bill.

But it gives you a sense of the scale. A billion dollar training run, plus all the experiments it took to get there, and then a whole lot more compute for post-training.
